HISTORY AND PHYSICAL (H&P)

History:
• Chief complaint: 3-day history of diarrhea.  
• Characteristics: 4–5 bowel movements/day; variable consistency (watery to loose).  
• Associated symptoms: mild, intermittent lower abdominal pain; single episode of vomiting; slight subjective fever; ↓ appetite. Denies blood or mucus in stool.  
• Hydration/nutrition: Maintaining oral fluids; no current signs of dehydration.  
• Precipitating factors: No recent travel, unusual foods, or known dietary triggers.  
• Prior episodes: Occasional mild diarrhea in past after certain foods, resolved spontaneously.  
• Self-care to date: No medications taken for diarrhea or pain.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma (currently uses a yellow inhaler patient calls “Lexapro” – medication name/dose/frequency not documented; conflict noted as Lexapro is ordinarily oral escitalopram).  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.  
• Allergies: None known.  
• Medications: “Lexapro” inhaler (details not documented); no OTC drugs.  
• Surgical/Hospital history: Not discussed.  

Physical Examination:
• General: Appears well, alert, oriented; conversant via video.  
• Hydration: No visible dehydration.  
• No other physical findings provided.

Impression:
• Acute self-limiting gastroenteritis/viral diarrhea.

Management Plan:
• Hydration: Encourage liberal clear fluids; start oral rehydration solution (Dioralyte) as directed on package.  
• Diet: “Soft” diet for 48 h after last loose stool (crackers, toast, jam, mashed vegetables).  
  – Avoid dairy (except yogurt/probiotics), meat, fish, and eggs until symptom-free for 48 h.  
• Probiotics: Yogurt acceptable to help restore gut flora.  
• Red-flag advice: Seek care if  
  – Diarrhea persists >7 days,   
  – Frequency rises to ≥6–8 stools/day,  
  – Signs of dehydration develop,  
  – Blood or mucus appears in stool.  
  → At that point provider will send stool sample and consider antibiotics or hospital referral.  
• Documentation: Written advice will be available in patient app.  
• Follow-up: Contact service if above red flags occur or if questions arise.

Patient Summary:
Mr. Michael John presents with a short 3-day course of mild-to-moderate diarrhea without alarming features. Examination shows no dehydration. Clinical picture most consistent with viral gastroenteritis. Conservative management with fluids, oral rehydration salts, and temporary soft diet explained.

Key Takeaways:
• Keep drinking plenty of water and add Dioralyte to replace lost salts.  
• Follow a soft, easily digested diet; reintroduce meat/dairy only after 48 h completely symptom-free.  
• Call back or seek urgent care if diarrhea lasts >1 week, exceeds 6–8 episodes/day, or if blood appears.

Next Steps:
• No immediate tests required.  
• Provide stool sample and re-evaluation if symptoms persist or worsen.  
• Routine asthma medication review at future primary care visit (inhaler name/dosing clarification).

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing expected elements: vital signs, detailed abdominal exam, complete medication list, family history documentation.  
• Internal conflicts: Patient identifies asthma inhaler as “Lexapro” (commonly oral antidepressant) – medication name uncertain.  
• Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional indistinct words but clinical data interpretable.
